speechtext: In reply to a question put by the hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton (Sir Sam Hughes) the other day as to the casualties amongst Canadians in the fighting around Lens, the casualties at the front in the Canadian Expeditionary Force so far reported for the period from the 16th to the 31st of August were 7,586. This covers the period of exceptionally severe fighting in and around Lens, where the Canadian forces were heavily engaged. The discharges in Canada during the same period for various causes were 689. This gives a total wastage of 8,275. The total recruits in combatant arms during the same period was approximately 800, making a net wastage of approximately 7,475.

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

subtopic: PAY OF SOLDIERS PROMOTED AND OF OFFICERS WHO REVERT IN RANK.
speechtext:
The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) the other day asked the following question:
I wish to ask the Minister of Militia whether it is a fact that men who have foeen promoted on the field in France and Flanders, and who, having been wounded, return to the base or to Canada, receive only the ,pay of the position which they occupied when they left Canada, while men who received their appointment in England or in Canada, upon being wounded, receive the pay of their present rank.
So far as the department is aware, men who have been promoted on the field in France and Flanders, and who have been wounded, and returned to the base, continue to receive the pay/ of the permanent grade held at the time they were wounded. Men who have received their appointment in England or in Canada, upon being sent overseas, and who have been wounded, would similarly receive the pay of the permanent grade they occupied in their overseas unit.
The above does not apply to men who are holding acting rank only. When men with acting rank are wounded, they receive the pay of their permanent rank.

Order. Unless the hon. gentleman wishes to deny or qualify -some remark in respect to himself he is not in order in bringing this matter up on a question of privilege.
Sir SAM IiUGHE-S: I will deny some remarks concerning .myself. The next statement of the hon. gentleman- was:
"When he oame to this country looking for promotion the then Minister of Militia refused to give him promotion, because he was not entitled to it."
Neither of the two -statements I have read is correct. I may say -that I recommended Colonel Currie for promotion- to the rank -of Brigadier General. Owing to the fact that rumours had been passed around concerning him by his enemies, I had -previously investigated them and found them absolutely without foundation in fact. There was no intention to hit Colonel Currie when these rumours were first started, but gossip -soon gets going, and it was decided to hold up the recommendation until a full report was obtained. Subsequently I recommended his promotion to the rank of Brigadier General and he acted .as Brigadier -until recently. Later on, Colonel Currie complained in the House that he had not been decorated for his splendid -service at the battle of St. Julien. That statement of his ih-ad no connection whatever, as I understand it, with my action in recommending him for promotion. I w-a-s not present when he made these remarks in the House, but judging by the Hansard report, he seemed to think that General Alder-son -and I should have recommended him for -s-ome decoration on the field. I explained in the House -that I had nothing whatever to do with that, -and would not think of interfering. So the -statements made yesterday in the House concerning Colonel Currie and myself are -absolutely without foundation.

speechtext: As a matter of general principle I desire to give every opportunity to an hon. member who rises to a question of privilege to make his statement, but as the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Neely) proceeded, it appeared that lie had reference to a difference between him and a gentleman who is not a member of this House. speechtext:
I was speaking as a public man, and I hiave been given the lie direct. That charge against my truthfulness has been published in the press throughout the

country from coast to coast. The statement I made in Chatham on Saturday last was to the effect that on the 8th day of June Sir Clifford Sifton, in an interview with me, pronounced himself as against putting conscription into force in Canada at the present time. In the Toronto Star of September 10 he, Sir Clifford Sifton, is quoted as making the following statement with reference to that interview:
I said that I regretted very much there was likely to he a split on the subject of conscription. in which different portions of the country would be arraigned against each other, but that it was quite clear to me that the Englishspeaking Liberals in the House ought not to follow Sir Wilfrid Laurier on this question. Dr. Neely asked me what I thought they ought to do. I said that they ought to organize themselves and repudiate the stand taken by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and at the same time announce their intention of supporting conscription and supporting the Government in its war policy.
That gives me the direct lie as to the statement I made. I made this statement outside of the House, as a public man, so that I could not claim the protection of this Parliament in making it.. In the statement I made I have the support of the-member for Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) the member for Quebec West (Mr. Power) .and the member for Richmond and Wolfe (Mr. Tobm). The hon. member for Quebec West stated over his own signature that at or about the same time Sir Clifford Sifton expressed to him exactly the same views as he expressed to me, and instead of the statement that he had advised me to organize those who proposed to vote for conscription on this side of the House I say emphatically that Sir Clifford Sifton told me to get the so-called eonscriptionist Liberals toogether and see if - there was no common ground on which they could support the stand of the leader of the Opposition because that was the proper' stand at the present time in this country.
As verification of what I say I have in my hand the signed statement of the hon. member for Quebec West which sets out that views similar to those expressed to me by Sir Clifford Sifton were expressed to him on the 7th day of June by the said Sir Clifford Sifton, .and that it was proposed to him that he should give an interview to the editor of the Manitoba Free Press who was to be in Ottawa in a few days. The hon. member for Quebec West, whose views on this question have never swerved from the beginning, .and who was against the application of conscription as everybody knows-

Now that the estimates of the Secretary of State are under discussion, I have a small matter to bring to his attention, as I understand it comes under his department. Some twelve or fourteen years ago it was thought well by the citizens of Brantford to erect a memorial , for the purpose of suitably commemorating the invention of the telephone, and perpetuating the memory of its inventor, Dr. Bell. The citizens got together and elected the following board of directors, which was afterwards incorporated by provincial charter in 1906 as the Bell Telephone Memorial Association: W. F. Cockshutt, M.P. (President) ; Lloyd Harris (vice-president); W.
N. Andrews; E. L. Goold; M. K. Halloran, Geo. Kippax; G. H. Muirhead; T. H. Preston, M.P.P.; F. D. Reville; A. J. Wilkes,
K.C.; C. H. Waterous; John Muir (treasurer); Geo. Hately (secretary). A prospectus was issued, and we waited on the late Government in the year 1906; I think it was. My right hon. friend, the leader of

the Opposition, was good enough to listen to our request, and grant us $10,000 towards the erection of a memorial. I presume it is so long ago that hon. gentlemen may have forgotten but we appreciate the gift all the same. I have here a record of the public bodies that contributed.
The Parliament of the Dominion of Canada gave $10,000, the legislature of the province of Ontario gave $2,000, the legislature of the province of Quebec gave $1,000, the city of Brantford gave $5,000, the county of Brant gave $500, the city of Toronto gave $500 and the city of Quebec gave $100. We have been upwards of ten years working on this memorial, and I am pleased to state to the House that it ie now complete and that His Excellency the Governor General will be in Brantford on October 24 next to unveil the monument. I desire to take this opportunity of inviting my right hon. friend the leader of the Government and my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition to be present with us on that occasion. I think it will be acknowledged by all that the invention of the telephone ie one of the greatest inventions of modern times. It is more in ordinary use as a commercial enterprise and for social intercourse than any other instrument. Dr. Bell is a man of the highest standing as a scientist. . He is now a resident of Washington, but spends the greater part of his summers in the Maritime Provinces at a place called Baddeck. Dr. Bell was a resident of Brantford during the early part of his- career. Hie fatheT lived there for about twenty years, and the 6on who was teaching at Boston used to pay frequent and long visits to Brantford. It was on one of these occasions the telephone was invented, in the year 1874. I think this is worthy of your attention, because the United States has made a persistent effort to claim that the telephone was invented in that country. They have set up a memorial in Boston to that effect. However, we have the statement of the inventor under his own hand that the invention originated and was developed in Brantford, Ontario, Canada, in the year 1874, and that the first long distance transmissions of speech over a telephone wire or telegraph wire were made in the neighbourhood of the city of Brantord, one from Mount Pleasant to Brantford, a distance of five miles, and the other from Paris to Brantford, a distance of seven miles.
Will my hon. friend describe the memorial?

I will give a description of the memorial in a minute or two. I
want to establish the fact that we are not making any claim which is not absolutely borne out by the facts. There are hundreds of persons living in Brantford at the present time who were present at the first experiments and who know that the invention originated in the city of Brantford. Therefore we have for nearly thirty years past called ourselves the Telephone City. The old homestead of the inventor is still there and has been acquired as part of the memorial. Originally half a mile of wire was strung around the house under the eaves, and the inventor telephoned to himself sitting in his own room. T^iat was the first experiment. After that the wires were run along a rail fence for about a mile, and then attached on telegraph poles, and taken into the city of Brantford. Then the two (long distance messages I have mentioned, one from ' Mount Pleasant to Brantford and the other from Paris to Brantford were sent. I think we are entitled to claim that Brantford is the telephone city par excellence of the North American continent, that the telephone was invented there, and that it is a matter of no small public interest to the Dominion that Canada should be recognized as the home of the invention of the telephone, which is one of the greatest of modern inventions. I have before me a recent report which was submitted to the directors on September 10, 1917. Perhaps I cannot do better than read a brief extract from it:
The monument has been completed, in accordance with the agreement made with the sculptor, Mr. W. S. Allward, dated September 28, 1909.
He has been engaged on this great' work for upwards of eight years.
The monument is composed of Stanstead granite with bronzes as follows. Two heroic figures representing humanity sending and receiving messages, at the left and right, and a large centre panel in relief, containing five figures, representing "Man" discovering his power to transmit sound through space, with a figure over him representing "Intelligence," and three floating figures representing three messengers, "Knowledge, Joy and Sorrow." Under this panel is inscribed in the granite: "To commemorate the invention of the telephone by Alexander Gfaham Bell in Brantford in 1874." In the rear of the monument is a granite fountain, and the whole is bounded by a circle of granite.
The association has raised almost $60,000, including the subscriptions I have read. Many distinguished men, although not contributing very largely, have sent us subscriptions, and have placed on record their appreciation of what we were doing. Inasmuch as they are mostly public men per-

haps you would permit me to read the following expressions of opinion which we have received from several who are well known in Canada:
Duke of Argyle: I fully sympathize with the desire of the citizens of Brantford to have a memorial to the eminent inventor of the telephone. I shall hope to see it when again in Brantford, for I look Sack with pleasure to my last visit.
Earl of Minto: Hope that great success will crown your efforts to do honour to Professor Bell and his wonderful invention.
Earl Grey:	The suggestion is a most excellent one, and will be glad to give it his hearty support.
Lord Strathcona : I fully enter into the spirit of the proposal for commemorating the invention of the telephone by Professor Graham Bell, and it would give me pleasure to have my name associated with it, and to aid in the matter to the best of my ability.
Sir W. Mortimer Clark:	Expresses cordial
approval of the scheme proposed.
Hon. J. P. Whitney:	Already in Brantford
you have appropriately commemorated in the Brant Memorial a historical fact in which Britons everywhere take great pride, viz.-the loyalty of the Six Nations to the British flag in the Revolutionary war. Your present enterprise is likewise of more than local interest, and we, as a people, have reason to congratulate ourselves that the first experiments with the telephone were made on Canadian soil near your thriving city.
Hon. Geo. W. Ross: I had the pleasure, perhaps I should say the honour, of speaking through the first long-distance telephone invented by Professor Bell, from his residence in the city of Brantford to his father's residence at Tutela Heights. I think it was in 1874. The telephone was regarded then as the production of a clever inventor calculated to interest the curious and novelty-loving people, hut no one dreamed of its possibilities for commercial purposes. I think you are doing no more than is eminently proper to place on record your appreciation of the invention and the inventor in his connection as a resident of your beautiful city.
Hon. James Wilson, Secretary of Agriculture, U.S.A.:	I am well .acquainted with Dr. Bell,
and am one of his admirers. I believe him to be one of the greatest scientists of the age, whose invention had done more to facilitate the spread of intelligence than that of any other man, living or dead. He is at this time absent from Washington, being at the University of Edinburgh, where he is to receive an honourary degree. .1 am pleased to see the Canadians taking this step towards honouring him. If there is anything I can do to facilitate the movement to honour him, I shall certainly he glad to do it.
Admiral Dewey: This project seems to me a very worthy one, and I gladly comply with your request that I permit the use of my name as one of the American patrons of the association.
John Joy Edson, Washington:	In Washington, where Mr. Bell has resided for many years, the highest possible value is placed on his services rendered to the world as the inventor of the telephone.
Mr. Bell is esteemed also in Washington as a scholar and a great scientist and benefactor 
in many ways. Moreover, he is beloved by all in Washington who are fortunate in having enjoyed his personal acquaintance, and who have been his guests.
And last but not least I wish to place on record the appreciation of His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, now King George the Fifth:
Ottawa, 13th September, 1904.
Sir:-
The application of the Bell Telephone Memorial Association as contained in your letter of the 27th June last for the patronage of His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales having been referred to the Governor General from the Colonial office, His Excellency was pleased to recommend it to the favourable consideration of His Royal Highness; and at the request of the Secretary of State for the Colonies, His Excellency now desires me to inform you that His Royal Highness is very glad to accede to the request of the association for his patronage.
I have the honour to be, Sir,
.Your obedient servant,
C. J. Jones,
For the Governor General's Secretary. W. F. Cockshutt, Esq., Chairman,
Bell Telephone Memorial Association, Brantford, Ont.
From this you will see that the present King, then the Prince of Wales, became one of the patrons and we have as distinguished a list of persons as has ever extended their patronage to any memorial in the Dominion of Canada. The list is as follows:	.

These are the names of the persons who have associated themselves with us and I am now pleased to inform this House and the country that the monument has been completed. It is a work of art second to none in Canada. I want to extend most heartily an invitation to all the members of this House and to all the senators, if they will come, and especially to members of the Government and the leader of the Opposition under whose auspices this vote was given, to come to the city of Brantford on the 24th October next and help us to

celebrate this epoch in the history of the city of Brantford and also commemorating the fact that Canada is the home of the invention of the telephone by Dr. Bell in 1874. Although Dr. Bell is a Scotchman by birth, his early days were spent in Canada and his father for upwards of twenty years was a resident here. I am sure that Canada will do itself honour in joining with us in celebrating this great event.

Before we leave the Department of the Secretary of State, may I be permitted to ask him if there has been *any relaxation of the rule about women crossing the Atlantic? Last May theTe was an embargo placed upon them sailing in passenger steamers and there have been a number of inquiries as to whether leave could be given to -women who wanted to go across to Britain. I understand there is a rule but I do not understand how it is applied or whether it is universal or whether there are any grounds upon which an applicant may get leave to go.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
The rule is very strict. I am not sure that I can precisely state it. There have to be very special reasons indeed to enable the authorities to permit a woman to cross the Atlantic. The British Government put in force a regulation to the effect that none can go except with the consent of the Canadian Government. I do not know if they stated to us just the reasons that would warrant us in giving consent but their great desire is that it be granted as rarely as possible and only in cases where real hardship would exist if it were refused. There has -been no relaxation of the rule. What it was at first, it is the same now. My right hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) would be able to better state it than I because he has had more to do with the administration of it. But I might give an instance of the way the rule does -apply. The British Government appointed a Toronto University professor- Professor McLennan-on the board of scientific research over there, a board similar to the one we have established here. It is a more or less permanent appointment, at all -events, a war appointment, but under the rule which existed and which still exists, his wife was not given a passport to go. That is about as extreme a case as I know of. I thought it was quite an extraordinary thing. There has been no relaxation that I have heard of and I am satisfied there has been none at all.

speechtext: Whatever garb he may wear the Speaker i-s always very genial, he is the highest type of -a gentleman.

I shall be very glad if the Government or our Speaker will furnish me with details for which I have asked respecting /the indemnities of deceased senators, because if the -full indemnity be not paid to the family to whom I referred, it would be a great injustice, as corn-pared to 'the treatment given to the families of deceased -members of both Houses of Parliament in the past.
I do not know that -we want to inject into this debate a question of policy, but I gathered from IHis (Honour's remarks that he would be in favour of having the Speaker's quarters retained in the New House. There has been some discussion in the press /and quite ia lot of agitation in favour of abolishing the residence of the Speaker in both the Senate and the House of Commons. Never having occupied that high and honourable position, and not expecting to, I do not know much about it and have not much feeling for it. But, as no doubt, the interior arrangements -in the new Parliament Buildings will be fairly well settled 'before Parliament meets- again, it might be well if the Government or the committee who have charge of the re-erection of these buildings would take into consideration this very important question whether there are to be residences- in the Parliament buildings for the Speakers. I am perhaps becoming old enough to support time-honoured customs unless they are shown to be based on error, and if there is room enough in the new buildings I am inclined to believe it would be as well to continue the -residences.

I am older
than my hon. friend. I have had forty years parliamentary experience, and I hope

that Mr. Speaker, whether for himself or his successors, will see that the new buildings have apartments for the Speakers. It would be most inconvenient, in my judgment, for the incumbent of that high office not to have his residence in the premises. When the House sits until five o'cclock in the morning it is most inconvenient for the Speaker to go to his lodgings outside of the House. Moreover, it is more convenient for him to have his office in the building, his lodging there, his family there. In my experience I never found any inconvenience arising from the custom; on the contrary, I found great convenience from the Speaker having his lodgings under the roof of the Parliament Buildings. It is the practice in England, and I should be sorry to depart from it. I do not know the views of the present Speaker, but I hope he will agree with me.

I was going to suggest, as the matter is being discussed in the press and the country and also to some extent among the members, that it would be a good idea to get an expression of opinion upon this question from the present Speaker, and also from hon. gentlemen who who have been Speakers in the past.
It seems to me their opinion, as they know the conditions, would be better than the opinion of others. As I understood the remarks of the hon. leader of the Opposition, I think it would be a good thing to have the residence of the Speaker in the new House of Commons, unless there be some very serious objection. I rise to ask if the present Speaker would care to make any suggestion as to what he thought would be the proper arrangement.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am in thorough accord with the remarks of the right hon. leader of the Opposition and the hon. gentleman from Carleton, and I may say to the hon. gentleman from Souris that I am pleased to give my views upon this matter. [ should think, from the point of view of the Speaker, it would be a very great hardship if there were no Speaker's house. I am a young man, and, I think, of average physical vigour, but I have felt the strain of the constant attendance, hour by hour, during the present session, and I am sure an older man would feel it in a very marked degree. The Speaker must change his clothing at the dinner hour, and when he comes to the House prior to the opening of the sitting, and when the House closes at night. That may not seem a very serious matter, but 3661
when you realize that you have to do that four times a day, and drive to an outside residence in all conditions of weather, it becomes somewhat tiresome and troublesome during the long sessions. There is the further fact that hon. gentlemen can get pairs upon all occasions, and go home to their families or to social engagements, but the Speaker is debarred from that, and must be always present.
There is another aspect which, I think, is of even greater importance; it is this: there is an atmosphere about the office of Speaker which I would be sorry to see this Parliament lose. There is a dignity and importance attached to the office in Great Britain which we, of course, cannot hope to attain in Canada, but which we should emulate. I am not referring to the social feature, but to the added dignity that lends itself to the office of Speaker when he has an official residence. There is also the circumstance that hon. gentlemen of varying shades of political opinion have the opportunity to foregather in the Speaker's house from time to time, which tends towards more pleasant and friendly relationship between the members, and as members thus come to know each other better, it, in my opinion, elevates the love of public life. My own view is-and I have given the matter very careful thought-that it would be a mistake to try to adjust the space in the new building to suit the requirements of the Speaker's House. In the first place, the ceilings are too high. It is doubtful if the partitions could be properly arranged to afford suitable accommodation. My view is that it would be a wise thing to erect an individual house for the Speaker on the edge of the cliff, which could be, while a separate house, joined with the main Parliament building by an arch-way or arcade of Gothic design in consonance with the building itself. By such a construction you would have all the advantages of an individual house for the Speaker. You would have convenient access to the Chamber. From an architectural viewpoint, it would add materially to the appearance of the buildings on the hill, because it is just a question whether, as the building now stands, it is not too rectangular. The Speaker's residence would break off, and rather improve, the perspective, looking at the hill from a distance. I have discussed this feature with Mr. Pearson, who is, of course, a very competent architect, and who has splendid artistic taste, and he is in thorough accord with my suggestion. It would cost more

to do this than to arrange quarters in the new building, but, as against that, you would have the added space in the new building, and, after all we are erecting buildings which ought to be suitable to the business of the Dominion for centuries. Bearing that in mind, it seems to me, for all it would cost to build a separate house for the Speaker, that that would be the ideal thing to do, and I sincerely hope that my suggestion in that respect will meet with the approval of hon. members.
To appoint Mr. M. F. Johnston to the Second Division, subdivision A, at $2,000 per annum, as reporter on the Committee Section of the Reporting Branch of the House of Commons, from September 1, 1917, $1,106.67.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
This is ia case which the Civil Service Commission are entirely responsible for, and I may say, with all respect to that body, if they had seen their duty as I think they ought to have seen it, this item would not of necessity have appeared in, the estimates at all. I might say in explanation that last session when the Senate re-organized its debates reporting staff, it was arranged that Mr. Johnston who had been one of the Senate reporters for 25 years, should be transferred to the Commons Committee reporting staff, to fill an existing vacancy. It was assumed that a certificate would be given by the Civil Service Commission. Mr. Shortt refused to issue a certificate but Mr. Laroehelle wrote approving the appointment of Mr. Johnston on his fitness and qualification. The letter from Mr. Laroehelle is attached.
Mr. Johnston was engaged for over two months this session reporting the committees of the Commons, and for nine weeks reporting the debates in the House, in both of which positions he gave satisfaction.
Recommendations as to Mr. Johnston's qualifications for the position on the committees staff were furnished by the editor of Hansard and the associate editor, and by the chief of the committee reporters, and Mr. Holland, late chief of the Senate report-ting staff.
In their recommendation, the editors of Hansard state that Mr. Johnston's appointment "would be in the interest of efficiency in the service."
Mr. Johnston has been for many years official reporter in the Ontario courts, and has had wide experience in such work. The appointment is to fill a vacancy; it does not add, to the establishment or the charge on the revenue. It was assumed that under section 21 of the Amended Civil Service Act the Civil Service Commission would grant the necessary certificate, but for reasons
[The Speaker.]
which I know not, they refused to do ,so. In a letter to the Clerk of this House, Mr. La Rochelle, the other member of the Civil Service Commission, writes :
Sir:-
In answer to your letter of the 2,5th instant, concerning the proposed appointment of Mr. Fiske Johnston to the Committee Reporting Branch of the House of Commons, I may say that I have carefully considered this matter, and that I believe this gentleman fully Qualified to fill such a position.
The Civil Service Commission has been furnished with statements and testimonials from the heads of the reporting staffs of the Senate and the House of Commons, establishing that Mr. Johnston possesses to a high degree the qualifications required to efficiently fill the position to which it is proposed to appoint him, and, furthermore, that for more than twenty years he has been actually discharging with the utmost satisfaction duties similar to those attaching to the position in question.
It is true that, as a general rule, the Civil Service Commission issues certificates of qualification for positions in the inside service only after actual tests of qualification, but, on the other hand, section 21 of the Amended Civil Service Act (1908) provides that in certain cases of a professional, technical or peculiar character, where it is satisfied that a person recommended for appointment is fully qualified, such examination may be dispensed with. And I am to state that in my opinion the present case is clearly one where an examination may be dispensed with and that the certificate required for the appointment of Mr. Johnston may very properly be granted by the Civil Service Commission.
You will understand, of course, that my opinion is not shared by my colleague and that as a result of our disagreement no certificate can legally issue under the law.
This is a case in which, if we did not take this action, a very grave injustice would be done to a very competent official of this House, and, nnder the circumstances, I am quite sure the committee will pass the item.
There is a deadlock.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Yes.
Mr, MARCIL: The Government provided some years 'ago for the appointment of a third member of the Civil Service Commission. If that appointment had been made this deadlock would have been -avoided.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I quite agree with the hon. member for Bonaventure, but that is a subject over which I have no control.
As we are speaking of the debates-and Mr. Johnston belongs to the Debates Branch-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Committee Reporting staff.

I might, perhaps, here interject a few remarks about the French translation of Hansard. There has been a

marked improvement in the management of the French translation staff. The committee will remember that some years ago I and the hon. member for Bonaventure and a few others who took a deep interest in having a proper translation brought the matter before the House, and changes were made, but, unfortunately, the Speaker who then occupied the Chair did not seem anxious to meet our views. In fact, he followed his own inclination, and >as he had, I suppose, no great sympathy for the French translation, matters went from bad to worse. I am bound to say, however, that since the appointment of Mr. Leon Germ as head of the French staff, we have had excellent translation of Hansard. At the same time, we have had the French Hansard distributed to members practically at the same time as the English version, with, perhaps, a few hours or a day between. A little delay does not matter, however, provided we have a good translation. My hon. frfiend the Speaker will realize that Hansard is sent to public Libraries in Europe, to countries such as France, Belgium, Switzerland and even Italy. In Europe, the people who have to consult our debates will naturally read the French version, because they are more familiar with the French language than with the English. We, who profess to have some love for the French language and who .are interested in the culture of it, are rather jealous of that translation. Mr. Leon Germ is a well-known litterateur, and he has had a long experience in the departments before becoming head of the French translation staff. For many years he was the secretary of the Hon. Sir A. R. Angers when he was Minister of Agriculture, and as a technical translator he has possibly no superior in the country. He has, on one or two occasions, been the President of the French Section of the Royal Society, and he is one of the French Canadian writers best known outside of Canada. In fact he very often writes in reviews published in France. But there is always a fly in the ointment. My hon. friend the Speaker will realize that the head of a staff should be protected against the intrigues of his subordinates. The orders which he gives and the discipline which lie must exercise in his department should be sanctioned, and it should be the duty of both the Speaker and the Clerk of the House to see that that authority is maintained. It is so easy with translators, who generally have served in journalism, to take liberties with discipline, that it would be
a pity if that staff, which has been so well reorganized, should lose its strength. I do not make any charge or accusation against any one, but it has happened that one member of that staff, whom I will not name, has simply discarded the authority of Mr. Gerin.
I know Mr. Gerin well. I beg the Speaker of the House to see that his authority is respected, because the moment there is a flaw in the management of that office, it will go to pieces as it did a few years ago.. As it is organized to-day, it is as near perfection as possible. I want the protection of the Speaker and of the Clerk of the House, both eminent gentlemen and men who value discipline, to see that Mr. Gerin's authority is Tespected within his own department.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am very glad to hear the words of commendation from the hon. member for Rouville. I cannot speak from my own knowledge as to the value of the work of the translators, hut I know the opinion generally expressed is that this work, in the past has not been done as well as it ought to have been done, and while some improvement has been made, there is room for greater improvement still. Bo far as my ability permits, I shall be only too glad to render every effort to that end. On the point the hon. member has raised as to the authority of one in charge of a branch, my experience in the business world before I had any experience in politics has taught me that it is an axiom of successful business management that you must give your foreman complete charge in the sphere of his duties, and that you must back him up while he is in authority. If it comes to a point of conflict between your foreman and those who are under him, you must choose as between your foreman and those who are under him, and it simply means that either the foreman remains, or his usefulness is done and he must go. So far as Mr. Gerin is concerned, his services have'been eminently satisfactory. While I happen to be Speaker he will always receive from me full sympathy and support along the lines I have suggested.

Might I ask if anything has been done towards helping the elevator men in the building? My hon. friend has been very kind to the messengers, hut the elevator men are after us nearly every day. They give us a lift, and they think we ought to give them a lift in their salaries. Of course, we have no influence with the Government, but I thought I would bring

to my hon. friend's attention the fact that these men are appealing to us. Remember also that the high cost of living pinches the poor man more than the rich.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: This matter has not been brought to my 'attention before. I think these men come under the Public Works Department.
But the Speaker is their spokesman.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I will make inquiries about the matter.
And about the messengers too.	1

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Yes.
To appoint Miss M. J. Barton to Third Division, Subdivision A, at $1,000 per annunf as a clerk in the Law Branch, $1,000.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I object as much as any member of the House to promoting officials by Act of Parliament as against the Civil Service Commission, but there are certain cases where a grave injustice would be done if a special vote were not arranged for. I cited a case only a moment ago, and I have now before me the case of Miss Barton, v horn it is proposed to appoint to subdivision A at a salary of $1,000, as a clerk in the Law Branch. I cannot put the case better than by reading a memorandum prepared on the subject by Mr. Gisborne, the Parliamentary Counsel:
Miss Marietta Barton passed the Civil Service examination under the law in force before the amending- Act of 1908 and came first in the examination at which she passed. She was first employed bn the House of Commons staff in 1908, and since that time was employed during the sessions on the House of Commons staff, and during the recess in various departments. I was appointed Parliamentary Counsel in the autumn of 1913, and Miss Barton came to my staff as my secretary in July, 1914, and she has been continuously employed in that position ever since. She is not only able to do my shorthand and other clerical work, but is also able skilfully and intelligently to look after the large amount of legal drafting that 1 have to do, as well as other legal work in the office. Unfortunately, she is now past the age at which she can go up for examination under the new law, but, under the peculiar circumstances of the case, I would ask that her name be put in the Supplementary Estimates as a clerk in grade 3a, at a salary of $1,000. She has been receiving pay at the rate of $900 for some years past. I would point out that I have, since my appointment, dropped two clerkships from my branch, one at $2,000, which was then vacant, and one at $1,400 caused by the death in action of the late Mr. John L. Godwin, so that the appointment would not involve any enlargement of the organization of the branch.
I am particularly anxious to have this proposal carried out, as Miss Barton is now only

on the temporary staff and her loss would he a serious blow to the efficiency of my -office.
(Sgd.) Francis H. Gisborne.
I can bear testimony to the ability, efficiency and industry of the Parliamentary Counsel, and in view of his representations I felt it my duty to ask that this vote be included in the estimates.

The Speaker states that this lady has reached an age where she cannot appear before the Civil Service Commission for examination. Would a similar vote to this have to be taken every year for this appointment?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I understand that this makes her a permanent official, and that from now on she will be in the same position in all respects as if she had been placed in the same grade by the Civil Service Commission.
Then she is appointed to the position by Act of Parliament?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is what it amounts to.
Once she is appointed by Act of Parliament, is her status any different from that of a clerk appointed by the Civil Service Commission?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
They are in precisely
the same position, I understand.
To provide a service of stenography and typewriting for the use of members-further amount required, $15,000.

I would call the attention of His Honour and that of the committee to the fact that $25,000 was voted in the main estimates for this 'purpose, and now an amount of $15,000 is being asked for, which makes $40,000 altogether. How many employees come under this head, and what is the salary paid to each?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I regret I cannot give exact information at the moment, as some of my papers have become misplaced, but speaking from memory, I think there are, at the present time, 42 stenographers for the use of members. The salaries vary slightly, but in the main the stenographers get $75 a month during the session. If the hon. member desires exact information on this point, I shall be very happy to send it to him in the course of the ddy.

The reason I ask is that I think it is worthy of consideration whether or not there should be a change in the system. I am speaking of my own individual case, and my remarks may not have any weight with other members. I occupy a

room with three other ex-ministers, and I do not find it at all convenient to have my work done by a member of the stenographic staff. I find it much more convenient to employ a private stenographer, whom I have to pay for the work I have done. I really think it would be very much better if an allowance, nothing like $1,000 per annum or $75 per month, hut something like $400 per annum, was made to the members, and let them, arrange for their own secretarial work. There is another objection. Many members have private correspondence to attend to, and for that reason it would be much more satisfactory to have tljeir own stenographers. I throw out this suggestion for the consideration of hon. members. I had the opportunity some time ago of speaking with His Honour on this subject, which I think is well worthy of consideration. The amount which is paid out, $40,000, is very large, and I really think that half of this amount allowed to the members would enable them to get their stenographic work done much more satisfactorily than under the present system. 1 do not wish to make any reflection upon the work which the stenographers have done. I think they are very competent and that their work'is satisfactory, but in my own case the system is not satisfactory. I do not know whether other hon. members agree with me or not.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I give only my own
views, of course, because, after all, the arrangement, whatever it is, has to be determined by the House of Commons. I may say that my views are entirely in accord with those expressed by the hon. member from St. John. When I was a private member of the House, before any arrangement was made, I always had my own stenographer here. I followed this practice until I was appointed Deputy Speaker. From almost every point of view, it would be more desirable if an allowance could be made so that each member might make his own arrangements. He would get better work done and would have the services of one stenographer who would become familiar with his methods. He would also have the advantage of his correspondence being kept in the strictest confidence.

In voting a sum of money for stenographers, this House is accepting the principle that it is right to pay for such service to carry on the political correspondence of the members. That seems to me to be reasonable, but there is no doubt in my mind that under the present arrangement the money is being used to pay stenographers to do a lot of private business for members. We might assume that each member would have about the same amount of political correspondence- that is not exactly true, but we may go on that assumption, and therefore we might make an allowance to each member to cover his political correspondence. Some of the members of this House carry on very extensive businesses, and I quite understand they might require more- stenographic services -than other members. I would be very strong'y disposed to endorse the suggestion made by the hon. member for St. John. As it is now, some members of the House are having more money paid out in their interests than others. We are all on the same basis so far as concerns the principle of paying for the carrying on of our necessary political correspondence. I think .it is reasonable that a certain, allowance should be made to each member, and let him supplement it if necessary, to get a stenographer who would attend to his business.

I entirely agree with the remarks of the hon. member for Frontenac. I believe I must plead guilty to being one of those who have employed a stenographer for private affairs to a much greater extent than for political affairs, because my political correspondence has always been very meagre, indeed, and it is practically nil at the present time. I have nothing but the highest praise for the manner in which the present system has worked out. The officials who. have charge of it are exceedingly courteous, and do everything they can to meet the convenience of the different members, at least thejr do in my case. The members of tlhe staff are also very courteous and attentive to their duties. I have had one stenographer who is a real artist, and whenever he is available I can almost take the responsibility of signing a letter without reading it over. Being a first-class stenographer, however, he is greatly in demand, and it often happens I cannot get him. I find when I dictate a letter containing some Legal expression, or some technical term, or sometthing out of the ordinary run of correspondence, to a young lady who has had no previous experience in that line, naturally she brings hack the work in a most unsatisfactory condition. I cannot find any fault with her, because she has not had the experience or training in legal matters. If this .amount of $40,000 were divided among the two

hundred odd members, it would allow about $200 each, which would be ample for a member who wished stenographic work done. If he had more work than that to have done, he should certainly pay for it himself. I believe there are many members of this House who would be perfectly willing to take this $200, and supplement it by whatever sum might be necessary, and provide their own stenographers, because in that way we would get much more satisfactory service than we are receiving at the present time. I wish to call the attention of the House to the last item, which may be' a personal matter to some extent, but perhaps we might jusit as well have it explained. Pertiaps the Speaker will tell us on what principle that item is made up. Of course, I understand there is one item of $2,500 for Hon. Dr. Beland with which every one will agree, but I would like to know on what principle the rest is made up.

The last item reads:
To provide payment of the full sessional indemnity of members of the House of Commons -days lost through absence caused by illness, public business, being engaged in necessary farming operations, or on account of death, during the present session, including an amount of $2,500 to Hon. H. S. BOland, a prisoner of war in Germany, notwithstanding anything to the contrary in Chapter 10 of the Revised Statutes, an Act respecting the Senate and House of Commons or any amendments thereto-payment to be made as the Treasury Board may direct, $22,010.
It is stated in the Act that members are entitled to fifteen days' absence without deduction from their sessional indemnity. If they are absent more than fifteen days it is deducted from the indemnity. The item explains itself to the extent that it is to pay members of the House of Commons who 'have lost days through absence caused by illness. We have some members who have been ill. I might mention the bon. member for Dundas (Mr. Broder) and the hon. member from Essex North (Mr. Wilcox) and the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. Guilbault) as being some hon. members whose names occur to me at the moment. Then, ministers and others may be absent on account of public business. It is also to provide funds to pay for days lost through absence on account of members being engaged in necessary farming operations.

I am a farmer, and I
was just wondering whether I would come under that.

About the month of May, the two Whips, stated there were a number of men engaged in farming, mostly in the
[Mr. Carvell.l
West, who wished to remain at home to put in their crops and look after their farming interests. It was understood that these men would be allowed an additional fifteen days. Tt was understood that those members who were actively engaged in farming would be allowed an additional fifteen days. That is the reason the item is worded in that way. Then, the other is on account of a death during the session. There is another matter that I might mention. We have had a long session, and it has been suggested by the Whips that fifteen days ought to be allowed in 'addition to the fifteen days that the statute allows.
That would be general?
That would be general. It is under the consideration of the Minister of Finance.

I would be much more in sympathy with the latter proposition than I would be with the proposition as it now stands in the supplementary estimates. I have not been entirely in sympathy with the idea that a member is a school boy and that he will receive pay, or fail to receive pay, according to his attendance. A man who is elected to Parliament must answer to his constituents, and if he does not attend the session and perform his duties, in all probability his constituents will settle with him when he goes back to them again. You allow a man fifteen days absence, and then, if he is absent beyond that, you deduct, I think, $15 a day. A deduction is generally made in my case, because I am away more than fifteen days during the session. Yet, I do not think I could be blamed very much if I said that probably I devoted ias much time to the public interest as any other member of the House of Commons. If I am absent more than 15 days, I simply have to lose the amount that is deducted. For a number of years the custom has grown up by which members are allowed a certain amount of leeway on account of illness. I have known cf men receiving some benefit from that provision in recent years that I thought was very shady indeed. 1 could hardly believe that it was a case of illness to the extent to which it has been taken advantage of.
Parliamentary illness.

Parliamentary illness, as my leader says. Now, we come to the question of farming. I do not know why the man who is away on account of being a farmer should be placed in a different

position from The man who is away because he is a lawyer. If I have courts going on, I must attend them, in doing so I am attending to my private business, and when a farmer is away he is away attending to. his private business. I cannot see much reason in making this allowance, and I think he should be charged for the time he is away like the rest of us. I am heartily in agreement with the proposition that on account of the length of the session the Government might properly allow an extension of fifteen days. I have always felt that special extensions are unfair and discriminating.

On account of the great.
shortage of labour in the West this year these members had to go away, and that is why this allowance is made. But the estimate brought down to provide for an additional fifteen days' allowance will be a general one, and we will all be on the same footing.

I have sympathy with the Government in the extension of fifteen days to those who have had to go West to attend to their farming work, although, as my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Car-vell) says, there should not be any exceptions. Each man thinks his business is just as important as the other man's. But, this year, on account of the great shortage of labour, I think it is quite excusable. I am thoroughly in accord with the proposition to extend the time of all members on account of the length of the session. But, I am not in accord with the idea of paying members who shirk their duty, who do not pretend to be here during the session, who only come once in a while when a vote or something of that kind is on, and neglect their duties for the rest of the session.
Department of Public Archives-To provide for the salary of the chairman of Publication Committee, $5,000 ; to provide for one clerkship in Second Division, Subdivision A, $1,600- $6,600.
Is that new?
Yes.
An explanation .should be given of it.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: In the year 1907 the Government published the first series of volumes relating to the constitutional history of Canada. The second volume, along the same line of work, was published in 1912. On account of the demand for the work, which came to be used in universities and schools as a text-book, in 1914 the Government undertook to republish both books, the previous editions having proved insufficient. Leading jurists were among those who made strong requests for the republication. Having issued these volumes, the Government considered the question of issuing collections of documents covering other important fields of Canadian development, including the treatment of the industrial and agricultural growth of the country. That is the purpose of this vote. The purpose of this vote is ito provide for superintending the production of these works. '
Is there a chairman?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: There is to be. There has been none selected as yet. The item was in when I came to the department. It is to provide for one chairman and one assistant, the chairman at $5,000 and the assistant at $1,600. They are to be known as the Publication Committee, and their duties are to collect and edit a series of publications following on from what has been done with the subject of the constitutional development of Canada, and commencing at the beginning with regard to the agricultural and industrial development. I am not sure that I am giving an explanation that is anything more than indicative to [DOT]the committee. The work, however, is not new. It is merely a matter of putting it on a systematic basis, and making some one competent responsible for its success.
Has the assistant been chosen yet?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I have not even heard the suggestion of the name of an assistant. I have heard a name mentioned for the chairmanship, but I am not at liberty to mention it.
I presume that the assistant would have to be chosen by the Civil Service Commission.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Oh, yes.
What about the chairman? Would he be in the same position?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: No, I do not think so. It would be unreasonable, a technical position-

I thought possibly there might have been some decision as to this point. A couple of months ago a lady spoke to me about a position something like this, not asking me to assist her in obtaining a position, as she knew 1 had no influence with t-he Government, but rather complain-

ing bitterly that the Civil Service Commission had refused to consider her application for a position having to do with the Archives, and I assume it must have bean this position, on the ground that about 160 or 170 years ago an ancestor of hers, in his official capacity, had played a part that had not been very friendly to certain people who lived in what is Canada at the present time. I thought if that were true, it was drawing the line very fine indeed, to cast upon this party -a burden which she should not be called upon to bear.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Visiting the sins of the father-

Not the father, the great, great, great, grandfather, because it yoes back about 160 years. I shall give the name to the minister in confidence. I was given to understand that the Chairman of me Civil Service Commission pointed out to the lady that, on account of what nad taken place in the case of one of her ancestors a century and a half ago, she might possibly not be persona grata.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I 6hall make a note of this, and so far as it is in my power no lady will suffer because her great grandfather committed any crime whatever.
Oh no, it was not a crime; he was a very high public official at that time, and carried out probably a very unpleasant duty.

I scarcely understand the necessity for this hoard. It would seem to me that the archivist would be the best judge of what should be published. If it is simply to deal with the question of what shall be published, I should like to know why we should have a distinct and separate board of officials for that purpose.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: The archivist is merely a collector. If Canada is to have her industrial and her agricultural as well as her constitutional records properly kept and edited, the archivist is not a man of standing to do that. I know that if hon. gentlemen heard the name of the man-
Is he a cabinet minister?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: No, I do not know of any cabinet minister who is anxious-
We were told that some were going out after the session to make room for new ones.
That is a false story.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: If I were competent I should like to undertake the work. I am sure hon. gentlemen opposite will agree that the party contemplated will be in a distinguished sense competent to do the work.

It seems to me the Government ought to hesitate about adding this office to the archives branch, especially when that branch is at the present time costing more than $60,000 a year, as will be seen from the list of officials in the main estimates, and the vote for contingencies. Now it is proposed to create another office and to attach a salary of $5,000 a year, together with assistants. I do not think this is the time for such an undertaking. These publications might very well stand over for a while. I suggest tnat for the consideration of the minister.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I have no doubt there is some extra expense in the archives owing to the extra efforts that have to be made now in connection with records for the war. Mr. Doughty went over to England and France a year and a half or two years ago and has spent most of that time over there in the pursuit of duties that peculiarly appertain to this office and that were quite necessary.

He is an exceedingly
good man.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: He urged very strongly that this opportunity should not be lost as the work could never be overtaken in the future. That may account for some of the expense, if there is an increase. This work is of a permanent character and if it is worth doing it is worth doing well. Literature that is not good literature is not worth producing.
Are these publications issued in the two languages?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Both languages.
